# Two implementations of the same thing

## Two packages, one problem

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**primarycensored**, R and Stan

- Density, distribution and quantile functions in R, plus a parallel
  set of Stan functions so people can fit in either
- The Stan half is the reason most of this talk exists
- On CRAN. `EpiNow2`, `epidist`, `epinowcast` and `distspec` use it
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**CensoredDistributions.jl**

- `primary_censored`, `interval_censored` and
  `double_interval_censored`
- Wrappers around a `Distributions.jl` distribution that return a
  distribution, so everything downstream still works
- Started a month after the R one and grew alongside it
:::
::::

::: {.callout-note}
You have just heard the case for a composable ecosystem. This is one
package's worth of evidence for it, including where it did not help.
:::

## Building the distribution

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```r
dprimarycensored(
  x, pdist, pwindow = 1, swindow = 1,
  L = -Inf, D = Inf,
  dprimary = stats::dunif,
  dprimary_args = list(), log = FALSE, ...
)

dprimarycensored(1:9, pweibull, L = 1, D = 10,
                 shape = 1.5, scale = 2.0)
```

::: {.attribution}
`primarycensored/R/dprimarycensored.R:69-81`
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```julia
d = double_interval_censored(
    Gamma(2, 3); upper = 15, interval = 1
)

pdf(d, 3.0)        # 0.1274
cdf(d, 7.0)        # 0.6677
quantile(d, 0.5)
rand(d, 10)
```

::: {.attribution}
`CensoredDistributions.jl/README.md:39-40`
:::
:::
::::

::: {.callout-note}
R takes the pieces as arguments to one function. Julia composes them
and hands back an object the rest of the ecosystem already understands.
:::

## Eighteen branches, or the type you passed

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```stan
real dist_lcdf(real delay, array[] real params,
               int dist_id) {
  if (dist_id == 1)
    return lognormal_lcdf(delay | params[1], params[2]);
  else if (dist_id == 2)
    return gamma_lcdf(delay | params[1], params[2]);
  // ... 15 more branches ...
  else if (dist_id == 25)
    return von_mises_lcdf(delay | params[1], params[2]);
  else reject("Invalid distribution identifier: ",
              dist_id);
}
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
```julia
function primarycensored_cdf(
        dist::D1, primary_event::D2, x::Real,
        method::NumericSolver
) where {D1 <: UnivariateDistribution,
         D2 <: UnivariateDistribution}
    function integrand(u, x)
        return exp(_logcdf_ad_safe(dist, u) +
                   logpdf(primary_event, x - u))
    end
end
```
:::
::::

::: {.attribution}
`primarycensored_ode.stan:52-77`, 18 branches, and a second table of 10
saying which of them have positive support ·
`primarycensored_cdf.jl:208-229`, where `_logcdf_ad_safe` is `logcdf`
plus one autodiff workaround for `Gamma`
:::

## Fréchet

- `cdf(primary_censored(Frechet(2, 1), Uniform(0, 1)), 3.0)` returns
  `0.847`. Nobody wrote that
- `Frechet` is not in the Stan switch, so in primarycensored it needs a
  new branch, a new integer, and a rebuild
- `primarycensored_cdf` has six methods in total, three of them closed
  forms for `Gamma`, `LogNormal` and `Weibull` against a uniform primary
- The other three take anything that is a `UnivariateDistribution`

::: {.callout-important}
The Stan file has to know every distribution it will ever support. The
Julia file does not have to know any of them.
:::

## Fitting

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```stan
model {
  for (i in 1:N) {
    target += n[i] * primarycensored_lpmf(
      d[i] | dist_id, to_array_1d(params),
      pwindow[i], d_upper[i], L[i], D[i],
      primary_id, to_array_1d(primary_params)
    );
  }
}
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
```julia
@model function double_censored_model(values, weights)
    α ~ truncated(Normal(1, 2), 0, Inf)
    θ ~ truncated(Normal(1, 2), 0, Inf)
    d = double_interval_censored(
        Gamma(α, θ); upper = 15, interval = 1
    )
    values ~ weight(d, weights)
end
```
:::
::::

::: {.callout-note}
`dist_id` is data. The distribution is fixed before sampling starts and
is chosen in R by a string. The Turing model builds `Gamma(α, θ)` out of
the parameters it is sampling.
:::
